extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students of American government and politics; general readers seeking an overview of federal regulation of commerce
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook chapter summarizing legal standards, administrative powers, and historical policies governing federal regulation of commerce (antitrust, immigration, tariff, postal, and executive/treaty powers). Intended as an instructional overview rather than procedural guidance for practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sherman Act applicability to territorial division among manufacturers
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a number of companies, engaged in the manufacture of some article, form an organization, divide the territory of the United States among themselves for the sale of that article, and suppress competition, the Act applies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court has held that when the direct, immediate, and intended effect of a contract or combination among dealers in a commodity is the enhancement of prices and suppression of competition, it is a restraint in that commodity (Addyston Pipe and Steel Co. v. United States).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sherman Act applicability to labor organizations' boycotts
rubrics_metrics.description: The Anti-trust Act applies to trade unions whose operations affect interstate commerce when, by use of labels, notices, or other means, they boycott a manufacturing concern doing a large interstate business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Loewe v. Lawlor held that such a labor organization becomes a combination in restraint of trade and is liable to the penalties of the Anti-trust Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureau of Corporations investigative authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The commissioner of corporations is authorized to investigate the organization, conduct, and management of corporations (other than common carriers) engaged in interstate commerce; to compel attendance of witnesses and production of books and documents; to administer oaths; and to require reports from such corporations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bureau's business is investigation of law and fact to furnish the government a sound basis for remedial legislation — not criminal prosecution — and to collect and make public information about great concerns engaged in interstate and foreign commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy distinction between 'good' and 'bad' trusts
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicists distinguish between 'good' trusts (those not attempting complete monopolies or unreasonable price enhancement) and 'bad' trusts (those constantly violating the law and endeavoring to create monopolies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This viewpoint supports regulation rather than wholesale breakup of corporations; some propose adapting existing law to regulate combinations rather than prohibit all combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: State vs. federal division of corporate regulatory power
rubrics_metrics.description: States create corporations and regulate their intrastate operations; the national government supervises interstate and foreign business of corporations without assuming the right to prescribe terms of their creation and continuance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exact domain of power belonging to each government is vague and the line between jurisdictions is difficult to draw; courts may annul laws encroaching upon another sphere but cannot fill the vacant sphere by legislation, producing calls for greater federal centralization in supervising interstate commerce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treaty supremacy in foreign commerce regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the President and the Senate's treaty-making power, a duly ratified treaty affecting foreign commerce is as much a part of the law of the land as a statute and will supersede any preceding inconsistent act of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A treaty might, for example, waive some provisions of a tariff act or add terms to the immigration law; the later expression of the lawgiver replaces conflicting prior law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immigration: Congress's plenary authority over admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress enjoys full authority over the admission of immigrants to the United States under the general power to regulate commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically the law shifted from encouraging immigration to excluding undesirable elements (disease, criminals, paupers, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for exclusion — 'generally undesirable' aliens
rubrics_metrics.description: The immigration law provides for exclusion of persons who are 'generally undesirable' including idiots, feeble-minded persons, epileptics, paupers, persons likely to become public charges, professional beggars, persons affected with tubercular or other loathsome or dangerous contagious diseases, criminals, polygamists, anarchists, and prostitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreigners convicted of purely political offenses not involving moral turpitude are not excluded if otherwise admissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract laborer exclusion and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Contract laborers — persons induced to migrate by offers/promises of employment or because of an agreement to perform labor — are generally excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: skilled laborers may be imported if unemployed laborers of like kind cannot be found in the country. It is a misdemeanor to assist or encourage migration of such laborers; actors, singers, and professional classes are not included in this group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese and other Oriental exclusion rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Admission of Chinese was broadly excluded by treaties, agreements, and laws, with specified exceptions (teachers, students, travelers for curiosity/pleasure, merchants and their lawful wives and minor children, officials of the Chinese government and their servants, and certain others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provision was made for authorizing and registering the admission of Chinese who fall within these exception groups; Japanese/Korean laborers were excluded by presidential order in certain circumstances (e.g., passports to Canada/Mexico used to attempt US entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration and non-reviewability of immigration officers' factual decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration of the immigration law, including the right to admit and exclude according to regulations, is vested in immigration authorities, with an appeal to the commissioner-general; the decision of administrative officers with regard to the facts in any case is not subject to judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational discretion is given to immigration officials at ports and to the commissioner-general, subject to internal appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immigrant entry reporting and tax requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Every immigrant must answer questions about marital status, literacy, possession of $50 (or how much), intentions regarding joining relatives or friends, nationality, race, calling/occupation, last residence, final destination, and additional questions; a tax of four dollars is levied on every alien entering the United States (with exceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete record of each immigrant is secured to allow government scrutiny; some persons (in transit, diplomatic officers) are not taxed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical and mental inspection requirements for admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Each immigrant is examined successively by an inspector for mental diseases, an inspector for internal diseases, and an inspector for diseases of the eye.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aliens about whom the examining inspector is doubtful are held for examination before a board of special inquiry at each port.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for appeal and removal of excluded aliens
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal from an adverse decision of a board of special inquiry may proceed through the commissioner of the port and the commissioner-general of immigration to the Secretary of Labor; excluded aliens must be returned to their homes by the steamship companies which brought them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative appeal path exists but factual findings by immigration officers are largely final for practical purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner-general of immigration duties and regulatory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The commissioner-general may establish rules, prescribe forms of reports and entries, and issue orders and instructions not inconsistent with the law; he must also investigate aliens detained in penal/reformatory/charitable institutions and look after deportation of aliens who become public charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He may detail officers at ports and oversee the administration to protect aliens from fraud and loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal power includes establishment and regulation of post-offices and post-roads
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress's power to establish post-offices and post-roads extends, in practice, to the right to construct buildings and provide adequate means for transportation of the mails wherever the public good requires it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some authorities argue this could include building and operating roads; others hold it does not extend, for example, to making telegraph a governmental monopoly or owning railroads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive federal control of mail transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: The transmission of mail matter is exclusively vested in the federal government; Congress can prohibit its carriage by private companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exclusive control coexists with limitations on what is 'mail matter' (see separate criterion) and on prohibition of private carriage of matter Congress excludes from the mails (see obscene/lottery materials).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition limitation of 'mail matter'
rubrics_metrics.description: What can be properly regarded as mail matter is limited to letters, papers, and other things which were commonly reckoned as mail at the time when the Constitution was framed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conservative definition has been used by the Supreme Court to limit the scope of the postal power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional exclusion of obscene/lottery material from the mails
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may exclude from the mails obscene, lewd, and lascivious literature or matter relating to lotteries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, Congress cannot prohibit the carriage, by private companies, of any matter which it may exclude from the mails (i.e., exclusion from federal mails does not automatically criminalize private carriage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal classification and rate policy for newspapers and periodicals
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress has made special arrangements for printed matter: newspapers are carried free within the county of publication (except in cities having free delivery); a bulk rate of one cent a pound is provided for periodicals entered as second-class matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second-class matter is defined as newspapers and other periodical publications regularly issued at stated intervals and 'published for the dissemination of information of a public character, or devoted to literature, the sciences, arts, or some special industry, and having a legitimate list of subscribers.' Publications primarily for advertising or free circulation are excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal grade classification of post-offices by receipts
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-offices are graded into four classes on a basis of receipts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Postal charges and services are tailored according to class; historical rates and revenue/weight share are discussed as context for financial effects of classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration and postal insurance service
rubrics_metrics.description: By paying an additional fee (ten cents), one may secure registration of a letter, a return receipt, and insurance up to the value of $50.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The registration service and post-office money orders (established 1864) provide guaranteed payment and reduce risk of loss in transmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postal subsidies and financial consequences of low periodical rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Bulk rates for periodicals (one cent a pound) are far below actual cost of transmission and contribute heavily to the postal service deficit; first-class mail contributes a small share of weight but the majority of revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate exists over whether to increase rates for newspapers/periodicals or to reduce transportation costs via revised contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracting practices for railroad mail transportation and calls for rate reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts between the Post Office and railroads have been criticized as unbusinesslike and excessively expensive per ton-mile compared to other carriage or to railroads' own freight charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An act of March 2, 1907, made provision for reduction in railroad postal rates; further reductions were being demanded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rural free delivery establishment and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Rural free delivery began experimentally in 1897, expanded greatly by 1908 (thousands of routes and millions served), and requires routes to be maintained in good condition year-round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incidental effects include relief of isolation in country life and pressure on state legislatures to improve public roads; Congress appropriated increasing funds as the service expanded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parcels post legislative conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When Congress established a domestic parcels post system (law taking effect January 1913), it fixed the weight and size of articles which might be carried and named classes of goods permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reform was long resisted by express companies and country merchants; the statute's terms limited what could be sent and at what rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department of Commerce bureau responsibilities for commercial intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Bureau of Foreign and Domestic Commerce collects statistics on foreign trade, studies methods to promote foreign commerce, translates foreign tariff laws, publishes consular reports, issues a trade directory, and investigates elements of cost of production, comparative wages, degree of control by business combinations, and effect on prices when required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These investigatory functions assist the President and Congress in tariff and trade policy; the bureau gathers factual material to guide executive and legislative decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department of Labor duties regarding labor, immigration, and welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department of Labor gathers and publishes information regarding labor interests and controversies, supervises administration of compensation laws for injured workers, supervises immigration and enforcement of related laws (including exclusion of Chinese), directs naturalization administration, and investigates matters pertaining to the welfare of children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Secretary of Labor may act as mediator in industrial disputes or appoint commissioners of conciliation when industrial peace requires it.
